title: Jaap Sahib
hook: Guru Gobind Singh's rolling praise of the Timeless, in quick changing meters

segments.voice: Yesterday, Japji at dawn, page one of the Granth. Your line was begin with japji. Did Japji get the first minute of your morning? Today, the bani that comes right after it. Day one hundred thirty.

You know how some music makes it impossible to sit still? A drumline at a parade. A song where the beat suddenly doubles and the whole crowd jumps. Japji is calm, like a teacher talking. The next bani in the Sikh morning is something else. It gallops. The lines are short, the rhythm keeps changing, and when a whole room recites it together it can feel like running downhill. It was written by the tenth Guru, Guru Gobind Singh. Today, Jaap Sahib.
screen: `A DRUMLINE, A DOUBLED BEAT.` → `JAPJI IS CALM.` → `THE NEXT ONE GALLOPS.`

segments.voice: Jaap Sahib is a long hymn of praise, about two hundred short verses, by Guru Gobind Singh. It isn't in the Guru Granth Sahib. It's in a separate collection called the Dasam Granth, the book of the tenth Guru, and it's said every morning in Nitnem and at the Amrit ceremony, when Sikhs are initiated into the Khalsa. It praises Akal, the Timeless One. And here's the unusual thing about how it praises. Much of it describes God by what God is not. The opening, in paraphrase: the One who has no mark or sign, no color, no caste, no lineage; whose form and shape and garb no one can describe. Then it rolls into salutations, line after line, each beginning with a word of bowing: salutation to the Timeless, salutation to the Merciful, salutation to the One without form, to the One without a name. Hundreds of names, most of them saying: beyond this, beyond that. It's as if the words keep reaching and keep admitting they can't reach. And the rhythm. Guru Gobind Singh was a poet as well as a leader, and he wrote Jaap in many different meters, chhands, switching from one to another as the hymn goes on. Some sections are slow and stately. Some are so quick the syllables tumble. The language mixes Braj, Sanskrit, Punjabi and even Persian and Arabic words, as if praise needed every language he knew. You don't have to follow the meaning to feel what it's doing. It's praise with a heartbeat, and the heartbeat keeps changing.
screen: `DASAM GRANTH, THE TENTH GURU.` · `NO MARK, NO SIGN, NO CASTE.` · `SALUTATION, SALUTATION.` · `MANY METERS, MANY LANGUAGES.` · then, large: `THE RHYTHM OF PRAISE.`

segments.voice: Listen for two minutes. If you can, play a recording of Jaap Sahib now. Don't try to understand every word. Listen for the rhythm: when does it speed up? When does it slow down? Tap the beat lightly on your knee if that helps. If you can't play anything, sit and breathe, and notice your own rhythm, your heartbeat, your breath, the one that's praising without words. The bell holds the time.
Jaap Sahib. Guru Gobind Singh's rolling praise of the Timeless, in changing meters, said every Sikh morning after Japji.
Your line: the rhythm of praise. Today, when you hear a beat, in a song, in footsteps, in rain, let it remind you of Jaap's gallop, and give thanks for one thing. Day one hundred thirty.

howItsDone: Jaap Sahib, by Guru Gobind Singh, is the second bani of the Sikh morning Nitnem and is also recited during the Amrit ceremony; many Sikhs know its quick rhythms by heart.

The authorship of parts of the Dasam Granth is debated by some scholars; Jaap Sahib is widely accepted as Guru Gobind Singh's and is in Nitnem and the Amrit ceremony. Stated without noting the debate; confirm the Keeper's preference.
Languages: Braj bhasha with Sanskrit, Persian and Arabic vocabulary (e.g., the Persian/Arabic names in some sections). Confirm.
